name: Bad Brains
label: SST
lede: Four jazz-fusion kids from D.C. heard the Ramones, played faster than anyone alive, got banned from their hometown's clubs, and left behind a scene that became Dischord.

eras.title: Fusion kids hear the Ramones
eras.text: Four young Black musicians from the D.C. area were playing Return to Forever-style jazz fusion as Mind Power until a friend put punk records in front of them. Within two years they were the fastest band anyone in Washington had seen, and the kids who would build Dischord were in the room.

years.h: Sid McCray turns Mind Power on to punk
years.p: Mind Power, with Gary Miller ([[Dr. Know|1cacaa8e-ba7b-408e-be51-6cc36b496156]]) on guitar, [[Darryl Jenifer|f82bc155-c490-4b5f-bc5c-8462ecbdef01]] on bass, Paul Hudson on guitar and his brother [[Earl Hudson|529a7b1b-f7bd-4c09-9f03-2227ab779a61]] on drums, get their punk education from singer [[Sid McCray|2bae3f10-4b39-46af-ab76-6e0defc73989]].
years.xp:
Mind Power modeled itself on Return to Forever and the Mahavishnu Orchestra. According to Wikipedia, its first concert took place in the Hudsons' basement.

McCray, from a military family that had moved to Washington in 1968, sang with them first. Paul Hudson moved from guitar to the microphone as H.R. and McCray stepped aside, though he kept riding along on tours.

years.h: A Ramones song gives Bad Brains its name
years.p: Mind Power becomes Bad Brains, after Bad Brain from the Ramones' Road to Ruin. From Napoleon Hill's Think and Grow Rich they take the idea of PMA, positive mental attitude.

years.h: One hour at Inner Ear: Bad Brains' first studio session
years.p: Bad Brains arrive late to [[Don Zientara|a495882b-4585-4295-9269-e30c63f279fe]]'s Inner Ear in Arlington and cut six songs in about an hour, including Pay to Cum and Black Dots. The tape circulates among tape traders for decades.

years.h: Bad Brains play the Valley Green housing complex
years.p: A Washington Post photographer, Lucian Perkins, stumbles onto Bad Brains at Valley Green in Southeast D.C. H.R. tells him where the next show is, and Perkins spends the fall shooting the scene.
years.xp:
Perkins photographed Bad Brains at Valley Green on September 9, at the Hard Art gallery on September 15 and twice at the Madam's Organ artists' cooperative, including November 11. The pictures became the book Hard Art DC 1979.

[[Alec MacKaye|bb05a948-ea44-4c9b-9d19-2a48f757ca22]], then 14 or 15, was in those crowds. He has said Perkins was lucky to meet H.R. first, because H.R. pointed him to everything that followed.

years.h: Bad Brains are banned from D.C. clubs
years.p: Club owners in Washington blacklist Bad Brains after their shows draw destructive crowds. The band answers with a song, Banned in D.C.

eras.title: Banned in D.C., bound for New York
eras.text: Shut out of the clubs, Bad Brains played galleries, basements and group houses, and the teenagers who opened for them became Minor Threat, SOA and the first Dischord roster. Then the band left for New York, and D.C. had to get along without its best band.

years.h: Pay to Cum · Bad Brain Records BB 001
years.p: Recorded in December 1979 at Dots Studio in New York with Jimi Quidd, the debut single puts 93 seconds of hardcore on one side and Stay Close to Me on the other.
years.xp: Darryl Jenifer says he wrote Pay to Cum as a takeoff on the Ramones, and that it started out slower and kept speeding up. Filter later called it one of the fastest, most furious songs ever recorded.

years.h: [[The Teen Idles|84e8d8bf-da21-4488-89e5-50a4c12ff4fa]] open for Bad Brains at Madam's Organ
years.p: Too young to get into most clubs, the Teen Idles chase Bad Brains around town and land a slot opening for them at Madam's Organ, the Adams Morgan art gallery. Dischord calls Bad Brains maybe the greatest band in the world in 1980.

years.src: Wikipedia: Minor Threat · Wikipedia: Washington, D.C., hardcore
years.h: [[Minor Threat|09037f07-42bc-46ac-a1ee-37f834451fee]]'s first show is opening for Bad Brains
years.p: [[Ian MacKaye|c12f644b-1066-4ead-b0dd-d0c380f5cca2]] and [[Jeff Nelson|51f7994c-949d-4dbe-89eb-2c33f42a5620]]'s new band plays to fifty people in a basement, opening for Bad Brains, [[Untouchables|16d88df0-a2a9-4b3b-87ff-84e90e312d40]], Black Market Baby and [[SOA|e54cb250-3502-4c32-9482-70488bd9a8cb]]. Every band on the bill is from D.C.
years.xp: By then Wikipedia says the Teen Idles had about a hundred fans and ranked second in the scene only to Bad Brains. [[Henry Rollins|656b39fb-979c-4c57-bb87-61d1a8eb38d1]], Ian MacKaye's childhood friend and soon the singer of [[Black Flag|9941a936-196a-4a62-ae53-a69cbc33f20e]], grew up on both bands.

years.big: D.C. built a scene around them. Then they left.
q: When Bad Brains moved to New York, the rest of us were pretty heartbroken.
years.h: Bad Brains move to New York and D.C. mourns
years.p: Bad Brains relocate to New York City, play CBGB constantly and help light up the city's hardcore scene. Wikipedia's album page dates the D.C. club ban to 1981, just before the move.
years.xp:
In New York they fell in with Jerry Williams and his 171-A Studios in Alphabet City, where they recorded through the spring and fall of 1981. Their shows became the model for what New York hardcore would sound like.

Back home the kids they'd inspired were left to run the scene themselves. [[Alec MacKaye|bb05a948-ea44-4c9b-9d19-2a48f757ca22]] remembers the mood plainly.

years.h: [[Faith|f735a867-9a16-451f-8f83-669ed42e2574]] open for Bad Brains at CBGB
years.p: A few weeks after its first show, Alec MacKaye's new D.C. band Faith is on the CBGB stage opening for Bad Brains. The set later comes out as Live at CBGB's.

eras.title: The yellow tape and the Rastafari road
eras.text: Bad Brains' first album came out on cassette only, and it still sets the speed limit for hardcore. At the same time the band had turned to Rastafari, and its new faith produced both the reggae interludes fans love and the ugliest episode in its history.

years.h: Bad Brains, the ROIR "yellow tape"
years.p: Released only on cassette by ROIR, the debut mixes hardcore at impossible speed with reggae. The cover shows the U.S. Capitol struck by lightning.
years.xp: Jay Dublee produced it from sessions at 171-A in May and August to October 1981; three tracks come from Jerry Williams' live tape. The cover art was by Donna Lee Parsons of Ratcage Records. The Decibel Hall of Fame inducted it in 2007.

years.big: A tour against Reagan ends in a note of hate.
years.h: H.R.'s slur and an unpaid loan on the Rock Against Reagan tour
years.p: In Austin, H.R. learns that [[Big Boys|fde1cff2-5a7b-4e8c-9666-110fa90500fb]] singer Randy "Biscuit" Turner is gay. According to Wikipedia, Bad Brains leave without repaying a loan from Big Boys and leave behind a note with an antigay slur.
years.xp:
The Rock Against Reagan tour put Bad Brains on bills with [[MDC|0f3c4d10-e541-46f0-a589-61ad701c6ce4]] and Big Boys. H.R. and MDC's Dave Dictor had an intense confrontation over Turner before Bad Brains pulled out.

Both Austin bands wrote songs about it: Big Boys' Brickwall and MDC's Pay to Come Along, a jab at Bad Brains' own single.

years.h: Rock for Light, produced by the Cars' Ric Ocasek
years.p: Ric Ocasek of [[The Cars|092b603f-eb4c-4958-b10e-02420de5885b]] produces Bad Brains' second album, which revisits songs from the yellow tape with a bigger sound.

years.h: Martin Scorsese puts Pay to Cum in After Hours
years.p: Bad Brains' first single turns up in Scorsese's New York night-crawl comedy After Hours. In 2006 it opens the documentary American Hardcore.

eras.title: SST and a phone line to Lorton
eras.text: On Greg Ginn's SST, Bad Brains made the record that pulled metal and funk into their sound and became their best seller. Its singer cut part of it from a prison phone, and within months the Hudson brothers walked out for reggae.

years.h: I Against I on SST, with vocals phoned in from prison
years.p: Bad Brains' SST debut, produced by Ron Saint Germain at Long View Farm, blends hardcore with metal and funk. H.R. is locked up on a marijuana distribution charge, so he sings Sacred Love over the phone from Lorton Reformatory.
years.xp:
It was the producer's idea to record the Sacred Love vocal down a prison phone line. Paul Rachman directed the video for the title track.

Wikipedia calls I Against I the band's best-selling album. Alternative Press put it at No. 9 in its top 99 of 1985 to 1995, and in 2019 Bad Brains re-recorded the title track with rapper Denzel Curry.

years.h: H.R. and Earl Hudson quit Bad Brains for reggae
years.p: The Hudson brothers walk out to concentrate on reggae. Dr. Know and Darryl Jenifer finish the tour with singer Taj Singleton and ex-[[Cro-Mags|9ffa627f-32c2-4cb1-bfad-00cf348abc70]] drummer Mackie Jayson.

years.src: Wikipedia · Wikipedia: Sick of It All
years.h: Quickness: H.R. returns and redoes the vocals
years.p: Recording for Caroline starts in 1988 with Taj Singleton; then the Hudson brothers come back and H.R. replaces Singleton's vocals and lyrics. It's now counted as an early groove metal record.
years.xp: [[Sick of It All|e204ed91-3684-4561-b29b-d0b53f8459a7]] and [[Leeway|121193a5-cb8b-4182-968c-8ba607856fa2]] supported Bad Brains on the Quickness tour, including two weeks on the West Coast.

eras.title: Four singers and a major-label shot
eras.text: The Hudsons came and went twice more, the singers changed three times, and Bad Brains finally took major-label money from Epic and then Madonna's Maverick. The last reunion of the decade ended in violence and a jail cell.

years.h: Ex-[[Faith No More|b15ebd71-a252-417d-9e1c-3e6863da68f8]] singer [[Chuck Mosley|9d2e1cba-9440-452f-bd00-999ecf1eb030]] replaces H.R.
years.p: After the Quickness tour the Hudsons quit again. Mackie Jayson returns on drums and Chuck Mosley takes the microphone, playing nearly 60 shows in the U.S. and Europe.

years.h: Bad Brains and [[Henry Rollins|656b39fb-979c-4c57-bb87-61d1a8eb38d1]] cover Kick Out the Jams
years.p: The D.C. expatriates reunite with Henry Rollins for the MC5 song on the Pump Up the Volume soundtrack.

years.h: Chuck Mosley leaves; Israel Joseph I takes over
years.p: Chuck Mosley exits in January 1992 and Israel Joseph I, born Dexter Pinto, becomes Bad Brains' fourth lead singer. Epic Records comes to Dr. Know with the band's first major-label deal.

years.h: Rise on Epic, with Israel Joseph I singing
years.p: Bad Brains' only Epic album. Mackie Jayson leaves in the middle of the tour and Philadelphia skater and musician [[Chuck Treece|ef661f53-d4b4-4903-811c-f3dcb1b970f3]] fills in on drums.

years.h: God of Love on Madonna's Maverick label
years.p: H.R. and Earl Hudson are back again. Bad Brains open for the [[Beastie Boys|9beb62b2-88db-4cea-801e-162cd344ee53]] on the Ill Communication tour and headline a U.S. run with a then-unknown [[Deftones|7527f6c2-d762-4b88-b5e2-9244f1e34c46]].

years.h: H.R. hits two fans with a mic stand in Kansas
years.p: Rolling Stone reports H.R. was arrested after striking two fans with a microphone stand at a show in Kansas. Wikipedia says there were violent incidents against the band's manager, fans and venue staff; H.R. went to jail and the band broke up.

eras.title: Soul Brains and a Beastie in the booth
eras.text: Bad Brains kept returning in pieces: old tapes, a name they could legally use, and finally a new album produced by one of the Beastie Boys, the band that had grown up worshipping them. The original four were playing CBGB again before it closed.

years.h: Black Dots: the 1979 D.C. recordings finally come out
years.p: Caroline releases Bad Brains' earliest recordings, made in Washington in 1979, as an album seventeen years later.

years.h: The original four tour as Soul Brains
years.p: Between 1998 and 2001 the classic lineup of H.R., Dr. Know, Darryl Jenifer and Earl Hudson tours under the name Soul Brains and releases a live album. The year before, they remastered early tapes as The Omega Sessions.

years.h: Bad Brains play CBGB one more time
years.p: Bad Brains play their first shows in years at CBGB, the Bowery club they had helped make, in its final year.

years.h: Build a Nation, produced by Adam Yauch
years.p: The first Bad Brains studio album in a decade is produced by [[Adam Yauch|0d3bf21a-5eec-443c-9a37-b305598b0840]], MCA of the Beastie Boys. Israel Joseph I fills in for H.R. on some dates of the tour that follows.
years.xp: The debt ran deep. [[Dave Grohl|4d5f891d-9bce-45ae-ad86-912dd27252fa]] has said he learned to drum by arranging pillows on his bed like a kit and playing along to Bad Brains.

years.h: Into the Future ends with a tribute to Adam Yauch
years.p: Bad Brains' ninth studio album closes with MCA Dub, for the Beastie Boy who had produced Build a Nation and died that May. Jamie Saft joins on keyboards for touring.

eras.title: Hall of Fame calls, bodies give out
eras.text: The hardest years of Bad Brains' story are the recent ones: a guitarist on life support, a singer in near-constant pain, two former singers dead. And then, from the tape vault in Arlington, the session where it all started.

years.h: Dr. Know has a heart attack and goes on life support
years.p: Dr. Know is put on life support over fears of organ failure. His bandmates run a GoFundMe, and he makes a full recovery over three months.

years.h: H.R. goes public with SUNCT
years.p: H.R. announces he has SUNCT, a rare disorder that causes stabbing headaches, and another GoFundMe pays for treatment. Rolling Stone later reports brain surgery in 2017 that helped only for a while.
years.xp:
Rolling Stone also reports H.R. was diagnosed with schizoaffective disorder in 2013; his wife, Lori Carns Hudson, has been his full-time caregiver since. In 2015 Bad Brains recorded the live EP The Woodstock Sessions with Jamaican singer Jesse Royal in his place.

Benefit shows at the Teragram Ballroom in Los Angeles (December 2023) and Brooklyn Bowl in New York (April 2024) raised money for his medical bills.

years.h: Bad Brains are nominated for the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame
years.p: The nomination doesn't turn into an induction. In December, Dr. Know and Darryl Jenifer tell Rolling Stone they hope to make an album called Mind Power.

years.cap: Sid McCray back with Bad Brains, 2017
years.h: Sid McCray sings with Bad Brains after 39 years
years.p: At a show that also features [[Lamb of God|298909e4-ebcb-47b8-95e9-cc53b087fc65]]'s Randy Blythe, Bad Brains' first singer, Sid McCray, joins them on The Regulator. Bad Brains haven't played live since.

years.h: Chuck Mosley dies in Cleveland at 57
years.p: Chuck Mosley's family said he died of the disease of addiction after a long period of sobriety. He was found at his Cleveland home, and police suspected a heroin overdose.

years.h: Sid McCray dies
years.p: Bad Brains announce the death of the singer who turned them on to punk in a Facebook post three days later. No cause was reported.

years.h: [[Ian MacKaye|c12f644b-1066-4ead-b0dd-d0c380f5cca2]] mixes Bad Brains' 1979 Inner Ear tape
years.p: Trust Records releases Are You Ready: The First Studio Recording (Inner Ear, March 1979), the one-hour session in Arlington, mixed by Ian MacKaye. Tape traders have passed it around for decades.
years.xp:
The six songs are Pay to Cum, Don't Bother Me, Black Dots, Migraine, Send No Flowers and Jamming at the Atlantis. Pete Lyman mastered it at Infrasonic.

Darryl Jenifer says the band's goal on stage was precision, like a finely tuned NFL team.
